Posted notice (photo or copy with date)
Complaint Log with resolutions
Written responses to complainants
Copies of substantiated CCL complaints and cover notices
Quarterly complaint review notes
Staff training sign-in sheets

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] staff, volunteers, consultants and contractors who have access to resident information
policies.purpose: To protect resident privacy and the confidentiality of personal, medical and behavioral information, and to set clear rules for who may see or receive it.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] treats each resident with dignity and protects their privacy in daily life and in records (22 CCR §80072) [C2]. Residents receive their mail unopened and may make telephone calls in private. Resident information is shared only with the written consent of the resident or authorized representative, or as the law allows or requires. This includes disclosures to CCL, the regional center and other agencies with legal authority to monitor the home (17 CCR §54326) [C31]. The Needs and Services Plan and its medical, mental health and trauma-related assessments are sensitive records (22 CCR §85068.2) [C8]. Records are locked and access is limited to staff with a need to know. [AGENCY NAME] follows the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164) to the extent they apply, and as good practice where they do not, including the administrative requirements of 45 CFR 164.530.

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable information about a resident's health, health care, or payment for care, in any form (paper, electronic, spoken).
Access limited to what a staff member requires to do their assigned job for a particular resident.
The person designated by [AGENCY NAME] to develop privacy practices, receive privacy complaints and train staff; the Administrator unless another person is named.
A signed, dated document by which the resident or authorized representative permits disclosure to a named person or agency for a stated purpose and period.

procedures: The governing body designates [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] as Privacy Officer, responsible for this policy, staff training and privacy complaints.

At admission, the Administrator explains to the resident and authorized representative what information is kept, who may see it and why, and how to ask for a copy or correction. Information is given in a way the resident understands (see IR-06). If [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity, the Notice of Privacy Practices is also provided and acknowledgment is recorded.
Mail: staff deliver all mail to the resident unopened. Staff open mail only at the resident's request or with their consent, and read it only if the resident asks for help.

Telephone: residents have reasonable access to a phone in a place where they can speak privately. Staff do not listen to, monitor or record calls. Any limit on access is treated as a rights restriction under IR-02 and never imposed informally.
Staff knock and wait for permission before entering bedrooms and bathrooms except in an emergency. Personal care is provided in private with doors or curtains closed.
Records are kept in a locked cabinet or in a password-protected system. Files are never left open in common areas, vehicles or unattended rooms. Staff log off computers when leaving.

Only the Administrator and staff with a need to know may view a resident's file. Sensitive items (psychiatric history, trauma history, HIV status, criminal history, immigration status) are shared only when necessary for safe care.

Before sharing information with anyone outside the home, staff verify identity and authority. Information is released only: (a) with a signed authorization from the resident or authorized representative; (b) to CCL, the regional center or other agency with legal monitoring authority [C31]; (c) to treating health care providers and emergency responders for treatment; or (d) as otherwise required by law, such as mandated abuse reports.
The Administrator records each non-routine disclosure (date, recipient, information given, legal basis) in the resident's disclosure log.

Staff do not discuss residents by name in front of other residents or visitors, in public places, on social media, in texts or personal email. Photos or video of residents are taken only with written consent and never on personal devices unless the Administrator has approved it in writing.
Fax, email and electronic transmissions of PHI use secure methods the Administrator has approved. Documents are checked for the right recipient before sending.

Records leaving the home (for medical appointments or relocation) are carried in a closed folder and returned or logged. Documents no longer required are destroyed by shredding only after the retention period in REC-01 has passed.
All staff sign a confidentiality agreement and are trained on this policy at orientation and annually thereafter. Training dates are recorded in the personnel file.

Residents and authorized representatives may inspect and request copies of the resident's records and request corrections. The Administrator responds within [30] days or sooner and documents the response.

Staff report any suspected breach (lost record, wrong recipient, unauthorized viewing) to the Privacy Officer the same day. The Privacy Officer investigates, limits harm, notifies the resident or representative, and makes any legally required notifications, documenting each step.
Violations of this policy result in corrective action up to and including termination. Privacy complaints are handled under IR-03, and nobody is retaliated against for raising one.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees privacy practices, authorizes releases, handles breaches and complaints, and ensures training.
Protect privacy in daily care, access records only as needed, and report breaches the same day.
Designates the Privacy Officer and reviews breach reports.

documentation: Signed staff confidentiality agreements
Staff privacy training records
Signed releases/authorizations
Disclosure log
Privacy notice acknowledgments, if applicable
Breach incident reports and follow-up
Access requests and responses

policies.title: Informed Consent and Decision-Making Support
policies.applies_to: All residents, authorized representatives, and all [AGENCY NAME] staff who assist with planning, health care and daily choices
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident makes, or is supported to make, their own decisions about their care and life, that consent is informed and documented, and that legal decision-makers are involved where one exists.
policies.policy: Residents have the right to receive or reject medical care and to be free from coercion (22 CCR §80072) [C2]. The Lanterman Act affirms the right of people with developmental disabilities to make choices about their own lives (WIC §4500 et seq.) [C38]. The resident, authorized representative and anyone the resident chooses take part in all planning (22 CCR §85068.2) [C8]. [AGENCY NAME] presumes each adult resident can make their own decisions and gives the information and supports needed to do so. The right to leave the facility at any time does not apply to a resident who has a conservator or other legal authority that limits it. In such cases staff follow the legal authority's terms. Consent, refusal and any concern about capacity are documented. This policy supports the person-centered requirements in 42 CFR 441.301(c).

definitions.definition: Agreement to a service, treatment or disclosure after the person has been told in understandable terms what it is, why it is proposed, the risks, benefits and alternatives, and that they may refuse.
Helping a person understand options and make their own choice using plain language, pictures, time, trusted people and other supports, rather than someone else deciding for them.
A person or agency with court-ordered or other legal authority to make specified decisions for the resident; the scope is set out in the order or document.
The ability to understand relevant information and to appreciate and communicate a choice about a particular decision at a particular time.

procedures: Before or at admission, the Administrator asks the resident and the placing regional center whether the resident has a conservator, guardian, representative payee, power of attorney or advance health care directive, and obtains copies. The Administrator records the exact scope of authority in the resident's record and flags any decisions the resident may not make alone.

The Administrator involves the resident, authorized representative, any person the resident chooses, participating relatives and the placement agency in preparing the Needs and Services Plan [C8]. Meetings are scheduled at times and places the resident prefers and use their preferred communication method (see IR-06).

Staff presume the resident can make their own decisions unless a court or legal authority has said otherwise. A diagnosis, age, or a disagreement with staff is not by itself evidence of lack of capacity.

Before asking for consent to a service, plan or disclosure, staff explain it in plain language, using pictures, demonstration, interpreters or a trusted person as needed. They allow time, check understanding by asking the person to say it back in their own way, and repeat as needed.

For medical, dental or mental health care, staff support the resident to attend appointments, ask questions and tell the provider what they want. Staff do not consent for a resident unless legally authorized and instead contact the authorized representative.

Where the resident has capacity, their consent or refusal controls. A resident's refusal of medical care or medication is respected as their right [C2]. Staff never withhold medication, aids, food or other basics as pressure and never coerce or punish refusal.

When a resident refuses care, staff stay calm, find out why, offer information and alternatives, and tell the Administrator the same shift. Where the refusal raises a health risk, the Administrator notifies the authorized representative, physician and service coordinator the same day as appropriate (see HW-04).

If staff doubt whether a resident understands a significant decision, they tell the Administrator. The Administrator documents the specific concern, tries more supports, and asks the resident's physician, service coordinator or IPP team for a capacity assessment or for help, and does not decide for the resident without legal authority.

Where a conservator or other legal authority exists, the Administrator obtains that person's consent for decisions within their authority, shares information with them, and still asks for and honors the resident's own views and preferences to the greatest extent allowed.

Where a resident with a conservator or other legal authority wishes to do something the authority restricts (for example, leaving the facility alone), staff follow the authority's terms. They explain the reason to the resident and document the discussion. They tell the resident how to ask the authority or court to review it, and tell the service coordinator.

For residents who are not under any legal authority, any limit on freedom of movement, visitors, privacy or choice is treated as a rights restriction and goes through IR-02. Staff never impose such limits informally.

The resident's advance directive about de-escalation, seclusion or manual restraint, collected in the initial assessment on or before the day of admission, is recorded in the Needs and Services Plan and honored unless it violates the law or endangers safety [C8] (see PCS-01 and BSP-02).

The Administrator obtains signed consent, or documents the verbal consent and witness, for: release of information; photographs; medication assistance; any behavior support plan; consultants' evaluations; and any plan restricting rights. Forms are explained, not just handed over, and offered in the resident's language or format.

The Administrator supports residents to make everyday choices: what to wear and eat, when to wake and sleep, how to spend free time, who to visit with, and how to decorate their room. Choices are respected unless there is a documented, legally valid restriction.
Consent and refusal records are reviewed at each Needs and Services Plan review and whenever circumstances change. Consent is re-obtained as needed.
Staff are trained at orientation and annually on informed consent, supported decision-making and the limits of staff authority.

responsibilities.duty: Identifies legal authority, ensures informed consent is obtained and recorded, arranges decision-making supports, and escalates capacity concerns.
Explain things clearly, honor choices, report refusals and concerns, and never decide for a resident without authority.
Makes decisions within their legal authority and involves the resident.
Supports the IPP team in decision-making supports and any capacity or legal-authority questions.

Scope-of-authority note in the resident's record
Signed consents and releases

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Communication Access
policies.applies_to: All applicants, residents, authorized representatives, visitors and all [AGENCY NAME] staff
federal: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act
policies.purpose: To make sure that no one is discriminated against, that every resident can understand and be understood, and that reasonable accommodations are made in admission, services and use of the home.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides care without physical or verbal abuse, exploitation or prejudice (22 CCR §80065) [C4] and protects each resident's dignity and personal rights (22 CCR §80072) [C2]. We do not discriminate on the basis of race, color, national origin, language, religion, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, age, disability, HIV status or any other protected characteristic, as required by the Americans with Disabilities Act, Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and California law. Interpreters, translated materials and accessible communication supports are provided at no cost to the resident. Each resident's communication needs and preferences are recorded in the Needs and Services Plan (22 CCR §85068.2) [C8]. The Lanterman Act's guarantee of services in the least restrictive setting that meets each person's needs guides our practice (WIC §4500 et seq.) [C38]. Where privacy notices are given under 45 CFR 164.520, they are provided in an accessible form.

definitions.definition: A change in a rule, policy, practice, service or physical feature that gives a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy services and the home, unless it would be an undue burden or fundamentally alter the program.
Supports such as qualified interpreters (including sign language), large print, Braille, plain language, picture schedules, communication devices, captioning or reading aloud.
Limited ability to speak, read, write or understand English well enough to take part fully in services.

A person competent in both languages and in the relevant terms who is impartial and bound by confidentiality. Another resident is never used, and a family member or staff member only if the resident requests it and it is appropriate.

procedures: At referral and again at admission, the Administrator asks the resident, authorized representative and regional center about the resident's preferred language, how they communicate (speech, signs, gestures, device, pictures), vision, hearing, literacy, and the supports they use or need.

The Administrator records these in the Needs and Services Plan [C8] and in a one-page communication profile kept in the resident's file and in the staff area. The profile covers how the person says yes and no, signs of pain or distress, and what helps them understand.

Admission decisions are made on whether the home can meet the person's assessed needs as determined under PCS-01 and SB-06, never on disability type alone, race, language, religion, sexual orientation, gender identity or other protected status. Reasons for any decision not to admit are recorded in writing and shared with the regional center.

When a resident or representative has limited English proficiency, staff arrange a qualified interpreter or translation at no charge for admission, rights review, assessments, health care visits, planning meetings and complaints. Interpreter use is recorded.

Residents are told their rights, the visiting policy and the CCL complaint contact in a form they understand (22 CCR §80072) [C2]. Staff use plain language, pictures, large print, translations or reading aloud as needed. They confirm understanding and record how it was done.

Where a resident uses a communication device, sign language, or Braille, the Administrator ensures staff are trained in it, devices are charged, working and always within the resident's reach, and replacements or repairs are arranged promptly.

Staff speak to residents directly, respectfully and as adults, address them by their preferred name, and wait for the resident to respond. Staff do not use ridicule, baby talk, slurs, or jokes about disability, race, religion, language, sexual orientation or gender identity.

Residents are free to practice their religion and cultural traditions and to eat foods that reflect them to the extent practical. Staff help arrange transportation and attendance where requested (see HE-04 and PCS-03).

The Administrator makes reasonable accommodations in admission, daily routines and access to the home, for example grab bars, ramps, visual alarms, schedule changes or alternative formats. Residents or representatives may request an accommodation verbally or in writing from any staff member, who passes it to the Administrator the same day.

The Administrator decides on accommodation requests within [FIVE] working days, or immediately if urgent. If a request is denied, the Administrator explains in writing why, offers an alternative, and tells the person how to complain (IR-03).

Harassment of a resident by staff, other residents or visitors on the basis of any protected characteristic is not tolerated. Staff report it to the Administrator the same shift. The Administrator takes action to protect the resident and, where it may amount to abuse, follows BSP-03.

Emergency instructions, fire drills and evacuation plans are given to each resident in a form they can understand, and the Needs and Services Plan notes any communication need relevant to evacuation (see SA-01 and HE-02).
New staff are trained at orientation on this policy, on using interpreters and communication tools, and on cultural humility. Refresher training is given annually and recorded.

The Administrator reviews communication profiles and accommodation requests at every Needs and Services Plan review and whenever the resident's needs change. The record of the interpreter and accommodation log is reviewed at least annually for gaps.
Any staff member who discriminates or fails to provide required communication access is subject to corrective action. Complaints are handled under IR-03 with no retaliation.

responsibilities.duty: Assesses communication needs, arranges interpreters and accommodations, makes nondiscriminatory admission decisions, and ensures staff training.
Use each resident's communication profile, treat residents respectfully and without prejudice, and report discrimination or accommodation requests.
Shares communication and language information and helps arrange supports when needed.

documentation: Communication profile for each resident
Communication section of the Needs and Services Plan
Interpreter and translation log
Accommodation request log and decisions
Written reasons for any non-admission decision
Staff training records

policies.title: Person-Centered Planning, the IPP and the Needs and Services Plan
policies.applies_to: All residents, the Administrator, direct support staff and consultants who help plan or deliver services
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident has a written, person-centered plan prepared before admission, in line with the regional center Individual Program Plan (IPP), and kept current as the person's needs, goals and preferences change.
policies.policy: Before admission, [AGENCY NAME] determines that the program can meet the person's needs and completes a written Needs and Services Plan (22 CCR §85068.2) [C8]. The plan is developed with the resident, the authorized representative, any person the resident chooses, participating relatives, the placing regional center and the person responsible for admissions. It reflects what is important to and for the person. It is aligned with the resident's IPP and the facility's approved service level (17 CCR §56005) [C23], and it meets the person-centered planning requirements of 42 CFR 441.301(c). It is reviewed and updated whenever needs change and at least as often as the regional center and Title 22 require.

definitions.definition: The licensing-required written plan under 22 CCR §85068.2 that records the resident's desires, background, needs, assessments and the services the facility will provide.
The regional center's written plan, developed by the planning team with the person, that sets goals and services; the facility's plan is aligned with it.
The part of the plan describing how staff will prevent and respond to crises, including de-escalation, based on the person's triggers and preferences.
A plan required when a resident has a restricted health condition under Title 22 that sets out the care and oversight needed.

procedures: On receiving a referral, the Administrator reviews the referral packet (IPP, assessments, medical and behavioral history, legal status) and meets or talks with the person, representative and service coordinator to learn the person's goals, preferences, strengths, routines and what the person wants in a home.

The Administrator decides whether the program, including staffing, the approved service level and physical plant, can meet the person's needs. If it cannot, the Administrator tells the regional center in writing and does not admit. Any need that would require a change in service level is referred to the regional center, since a level can change only on a change of ownership or when most residents' ID teams identify a new need [C23].

Before admission, the Administrator completes the written Needs and Services Plan [C8] including: the resident's desires and background; the circumstances of entrance to the facility; specific service needs; mental and emotional functioning; and the facility's plan to meet each need.

The Administrator obtains and files the written medical assessment, normally from a physician, and the functional capabilities assessment under Title 22. Where there has been a mental health intake assessment, a copy is filed.

On or before the day of admission, the Administrator completes the initial assessment required by Health and Safety Code §1180.4(a), with input from the resident, authorized representative and any person the resident chooses. It includes: the resident's advance directive on de-escalation, seclusion or manual restraint (honored unless it violates the law or endangers safety); early warning signs and triggers; calming techniques that work; medical conditions that raise restraint risk; and trauma history.
The Administrator prepares the individual emergency intervention plan for the resident and keeps it with the plan so every shift can use it (see BSP-01 and BSP-02).

If the resident has a restricted health condition under Title 22, the Administrator ensures the Restricted Health Condition Care Plan is included and shared with nursing and medical providers (see HW-02).

The Administrator records the resident's communication profile, choices about daily routines, community interests, work or day-program goals, social relationships, religion and culture, and rights modifications (if any, through IR-02) in the plan.

The Administrator reviews the draft plan with the resident and representative in a way they understand (IR-06), invites changes and records their agreement or objections. The resident or representative signs, and gets a copy if they wish.

The plan is shared as needed with the regional center service coordinator and with direct support staff. Staff sign that they have read the parts relevant to their work before working alone with the resident.

The Administrator coordinates with the service coordinator and the IPP team. The Administrator identifies the IPP objectives assigned to the facility, builds them into the plan with clear steps, who does what and by when, and attends IPP meetings or provides written input.

The Administrator reviews each plan after any significant change (illness, hospitalization, behavior incident, change in medications, change in goals, family change, rights restriction) and at least [every six months]. The review is dated and signed with the resident's participation.
When the plan changes, the Administrator updates the plan, informs the resident, representative and service coordinator, retrains staff on the changes, and removes outdated versions from use.
The Administrator reports to the regional center, within the time the regional center sets, any resident need that the program can no longer meet, and starts planning under PCS-04 if needed.
Plans are stored in the resident's confidential record (IR-04, REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Determines the program can meet the need, completes and updates the plan, coordinates with the IPP team, and trains staff on it.
Takes part in planning, states preferences and goals, and reviews and agrees to the plan.
Convenes the IPP, shares assessments, and coordinates the facility's role in the IPP.
Read and follow the plan, report changes in needs or preferences.

policies.title: Implementation of Supports, Consumer Notes and Progress Reports
policies.applies_to: The Administrator, direct support staff and consultants who deliver or document services for residents
policies.purpose: To make sure supports in each resident's plan are actually delivered, that ongoing consumer notes are kept, and that timely progress reports reach the regional center.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] delivers the supports in each resident's Needs and Services Plan and IPP as set out in the approved program design (17 CCR §56013) [C25]. The Administrator ensures that ongoing consumer notes are kept covering community and leisure activities, overnight visits away from the home, illness, special incident reports, and medical and dental visits. Entries are dated and signed. Progress reports are sent to the service coordinator on the schedule below, within 30 days after the end of the reporting period. Program preparation time (2 to 7 hours per resident per week) is counted toward staffing only as 17 CCR §56004 allows [C22]. Documentation supports the person-centered services required by 42 CFR 441.301(c).

definitions.definition: Dated, signed, factual entries made by staff recording what was provided to or happened with a resident.
A written summary to the regional center of the resident's progress on plan and IPP objectives, health, behavior, activities and any needs or concerns.
Time spent preparing for and arranging resident supports (planning activities, training, coordination), which can count toward staffing within Title 17 limits.
A report to the regional center of a reportable event under Title 17, handled under BSP-04.

procedures: At admission and each plan update, the Administrator turns each goal and support in the Needs and Services Plan and IPP into daily or weekly tasks on the staff support schedule, naming who is responsible and how success is recorded.

At each shift change, the outgoing and incoming staff review the schedule and any new instructions. Staff carry out the supports exactly as written and offer the resident real choices in how they are carried out.

For every resident, staff make a consumer note each shift or day in which something notable occurs. Entries are factual, in blue or black ink or in the approved electronic system, with the date, time, and the staff member's full signature or initials with a signature on file. Corrections are made by single line strike-through, initialed and dated, never by erasing.

Consumer notes cover, at minimum: community and leisure activities; overnight visits away from the home and return; illness and symptoms, and what was done; special incidents and the SIR reference; medical and dental visits with findings and follow-up; behavior and responses to supports; and progress on plan objectives.

Staff record changes in condition and any concern the same shift and notify the Administrator as required by HW-04. An event that may require a special incident report or a report to CCL is handled under BSP-04 and REC-02 without waiting for the progress report.
The Administrator reviews consumer notes at least weekly, initials the review, and follows up on gaps, missed supports, patterns or needed changes to the plan.

The Administrator prepares progress reports on this schedule: semiannually (twice a year) for Level 2 and 3 residents, and quarterly for Level 4 residents. For Level 5 and 6 residents, the Administrator uses the frequency in the facility's approved program design and any direction from the vendoring regional center, and confirms the requirement in writing with the regional center before the first report is due.
Each report is sent to the resident's service coordinator within 30 days after the end of the quarter or reporting period. The Administrator logs the due date and date sent, and keeps a copy.

Reports are written from the consumer notes and plan objectives. They state progress on each objective with examples, health status, behavioral supports and outcomes, community integration and employment activities, rights restrictions, family contact and concerns or requests for the IPP team. The resident and representative are given the chance to review and add their views.

If the resident is missing progress, or supports are not working, the Administrator calls a plan review with the resident, representative and service coordinator rather than waiting for the next report (PCS-01).

The Administrator tracks program preparation time each week, recording who did what for each resident. Only time that fits 17 CCR §56004 is counted toward required staffing hours [C22]. Time for administrative, bookkeeping or non-resident-related tasks is never counted.

The Administrator checks monthly that staffing and any added weekly direct-care or consultant hours required for each resident's service level are actually provided, and keeps schedules and time records as proof (see STF-01).

The Administrator checks that all required items in the approved program design, including the sample schedule, orientation and training plan, and staff duty statements, are in practice [C25] (see SB-04).
Documentation is kept in the resident's record under REC-01, kept at least five years, and available for monitoring by CCL and the regional center (GOV-06).
Staff are trained at orientation and annually in note writing: facts not opinions, no judgmental language, protect privacy (IR-04).

responsibilities.duty: Assigns supports, reviews notes weekly, writes and sends progress reports on time, tracks program preparation hours.
Deliver supports as planned, write dated and signed notes, and report changes and incidents.
Receives reports, follows up on concerns, and reconvenes the IPP team as needed.

Support schedules and task sheets
Weekly Administrator review sign-off
Progress reports with date sent
Report due-date tracking log
Program preparation time records
Staffing and hours schedules

policies.title: Community Integration and Employment Choice
policies.applies_to: Administrator, direct support staff, all individuals served and their authorized representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure each person living at [AGENCY NAME] has real opportunities to take part in the community, to choose how they spend their time, and to choose employment and day-program options. These supports must match the person's Individual Program Plan (IPP), the facility's written program design and the person's personal rights.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supports each individual to live as an active member of the community, as an adult with the same freedoms as others. The facility's program design (17 CCR §56013, C25) describes the services we provide and the outcomes we pursue, including community participation, and staff carry out those services as written. Individuals may leave the facility at any time. Curfews and house rules apply only as allowed by 22 CCR §80072 (C2), and they do not apply to an individual who has a conservator or other legal authority that governs this right. Individuals are never locked in any room or in the premises. Individuals may receive visitors under the visiting policy given to them at admission and posted in the facility. Employment and day-program choices named in the IPP are supported by facility staff, including schedule and transportation support. Community and leisure activities are documented in consumer notes. This policy supports the HCBS settings expectations of 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4) and 42 CFR 441.710.

definitions.definition: Full access to the greater community, including the opportunity to work, shop, worship, use public services, spend time with people who do not have disabilities, and take part in community life as other adults do.
Dated, signed staff entries that record services delivered, activities, and the individual's response and progress. See PCS-02.
A person legally authorized to act for an individual, such as a conservator or a person named in a legal document.
The Individual Program Plan developed by the regional center with the individual, which states goals and services, including day and employment services.

procedures: At admission, the Administrator reviews the individual's IPP and Needs and Services Plan to find community, social, spiritual, day-program and employment goals, and records them on the individual's activity support sheet.

At admission, the Administrator personally gives the individual and authorized representative the list of personal rights and the visiting policy and explains them in plain language and in the person's preferred communication method. The rights and the visiting policy are posted in a prominent common area.

The Administrator explains to the individual that they may leave the facility at any time and may receive visitors. Any house rule or curfew is written, applies equally to all residents, and is limited to what 22 CCR §80072 allows. A curfew or house rule is never applied to restrict the rights of an individual with legal authority governing this right, and is never used as punishment.

Within 30 days of admission, and at least every six months afterward, direct support staff meet with each individual to ask what they like to do, where they want to go, who they want to see, and what they want to try. Staff record the answers in the individual's activity preferences.
Staff build a weekly activity schedule with each individual from those preferences. The schedule is flexible, is not the same for every resident, and is changed whenever the individual asks.

Staff help each individual take part in activities in the community, such as shopping, restaurants, recreation, volunteering, faith communities, clubs, libraries and other public places. Staff provide transportation or arrange public transit under HE-05.

Staff scheduling must allow community outings. The Administrator checks the schedule weekly so that outings are not canceled for convenience or staffing reasons. If an outing must be postponed for health or safety reasons, the staff person records the reason and the make-up date in the consumer notes.

Staff help individuals keep and build relationships with family, friends and other people of their choice, including help with phone calls, video calls, mail, invitations and transportation to visit. Staff also help individuals take part in activities outside the home with people who do not have disabilities.

Where the IPP identifies employment or a day program, the Administrator contacts the service coordinator within 10 business days of admission, or of any IPP change, to confirm the service provider, schedule and transportation. The individual's choice of provider is honored.

Staff support the individual to go to work or day program on time and prepared. If the individual needs support with employment, such as job exploration, applications, interviews, transit training or workplace supports, the Administrator raises it with the service coordinator and records the request.
The facility does not require an individual to take part in any particular activity or program, and does not condition meals, privileges, visits or outings on attendance or compliance.

The facility does not pay an individual less than required by law for work, and does not require chores or facility work as a condition of residence. Any household tasks an individual chooses are voluntary and are recorded in the person-centered plan.

After each community activity, outing, visit, work shift or day-program day, the staff person records in consumer notes the date, activity, level of support given, the individual's reaction, and anything to follow up on.

Each month, the Administrator reviews the consumer notes for each individual. If an individual has had few community activities or has repeatedly missed day-program or work attendance, the Administrator contacts the individual, talks with them about what they want, and removes barriers such as transportation, staffing or health.

Before any limit on going out, visits, or access to places or people is put in place, the Administrator follows IR-02. The limit must be supported by an assessed need, documented in the person-centered plan, and agreed to in writing as that policy requires.
The Administrator reports community participation trends and barriers to the service coordinator at each IPP review and to the quality improvement review under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure the program design's community participation outcomes are carried out, reviews consumer notes monthly, coordinates with the service coordinator on employment and day-program choices, and enforces that rights and the visiting policy are honored.
Help individuals take part in the activities they choose, provide or arrange transportation, honor the right to leave and to have visitors, and document activities in consumer notes.
Tell staff their preferences, take part in planning, and raise concerns about community access with the Administrator or service coordinator.
Coordinates the IPP, day and employment services, and the individual's service goals with the facility.

documentation: Activity preferences and weekly activity schedule for each individual
Consumer notes recording community and leisure activities, visits, work and day-program attendance
Signed acknowledgment that the individual and authorized representative received the list of personal rights and the visiting policy
Posted copy of the personal rights and visiting policy (verified in the monthly environment check)
Contacts with the service coordinator about employment and day-program services
Monthly Administrator review of community participation

policies.title: Transition, Discharge and Termination of Services
policies.applies_to: Administrator, direct support staff, individuals served and their authorized representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure any move, discharge or end of services at [AGENCY NAME] is planned with the individual, the authorized representative and the regional center, is not discriminatory, protects the individual's health, safety and belongings, and is documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows the entrance and exit criteria written in its program design (17 CCR §56013, C25). Individuals may move out as provided in their admission agreement, and any move is planned with the individual, the authorized representative and the regional center service coordinator. The rate and refund policy is stated in the plan of operation (22 CCR §80022, C16) and the admission agreement, and refunds are made according to them. The facility bills the regional center only for authorized services actually delivered, and the regional center rate is payment in full (17 CCR §54326, C31). The facility does not discharge or end services because of an individual's disability alone and considers reasonable accommodations and added supports first, consistent with the ADA and 42 CFR 441.301(c). The facility records the transition plan and where the individual's belongings and funds went.

definitions.definition: The written conditions in the program design describing who the facility can serve and when the facility can no longer meet a person's needs.
A written plan for a planned move that covers the receiving setting, supports, health information, belongings, funds, transportation and follow-up.
A move made at once because of an immediate threat to health or safety, such as hospitalization or an evacuation.
The regional center staff person responsible for the individual's IPP and placement.

procedures: The Administrator gives each individual and authorized representative the admission agreement, which states the move-out terms, the rate and refund policy and the circumstances in which services may end, and reviews these in plain language before admission. A signed acknowledgment is kept in the record.

When an individual or authorized representative says they want to move, the staff person who hears it tells the Administrator the same day. The Administrator meets with the individual within 3 business days to understand the reasons, offer solutions, and explain the options and rights.

The Administrator notifies the service coordinator within 2 business days of any request to move or of any decision to consider ending services, and invites the service coordinator, individual, authorized representative and others the individual chooses to a planning meeting.

If [AGENCY NAME] believes it can no longer meet an individual's needs, the Administrator first compares the situation with the exit criteria in the program design, then documents what supports, services, staffing, consultants or modifications have been tried or could be tried. The Administrator reviews the Needs and Services Plan and discusses options with the service coordinator before taking any further step.

A discharge or termination is never based on disability alone, on an individual's exercise of rights, on filing a complaint, or on the individual's choice to change service providers. The Administrator documents the specific reasons and the efforts made to keep the individual.

Any notice of termination is given in writing to the individual, the authorized representative and the service coordinator, in a form and language they understand, within the time stated in the admission agreement and required by law. The notice states the reason, the effective date and how to raise concerns or file a complaint under IR-03.

The planning meeting produces a written transition plan naming the receiving setting, the move date, who will provide transportation, how the individual will visit the new setting beforehand where possible, and the supports staff will give.

Before the move, the Administrator reviews the individual's medications, health needs, equipment and appointments with the physician and any nursing consultant, and prepares a current health summary, medication list and emergency contacts to give to the receiving provider with the individual's consent.

On the move date, a staff person and the individual (and the authorized representative if present) inventory the individual's belongings and personal funds against the property record. Everything is returned to the individual or authorized representative and signed for, following SB-08. Medications are sent following HW-01.

Staff make sure the individual's personal funds, trust balances, benefit information and important documents (identification, benefit cards) go with the individual, and record the amounts and the receiving person's signature.

The Administrator calculates any refund or charge strictly under the rate and refund policy in the plan of operation and the admission agreement, gives a written statement, and returns any refund due within the time stated in those documents.

The Administrator tells the regional center the individual's departure date so that billing ends on the correct date. The facility bills only for authorized services actually delivered through the last day of service. It does not bill for any period after departure and does not charge the individual or family more than the authorized amount.

For an emergency transfer, such as a hospital admission, staff follow HW-04, notify the authorized representative and service coordinator immediately, and send current medications and health information with the individual. The Administrator decides within the timeframes of the admission agreement whether the individual will return and documents it.
If an individual dies, staff follow HW-05 instead of this policy.

Within 10 business days after the move, the Administrator contacts the service coordinator to confirm the individual's transition went well, documents any follow-up, and completes the closing note in the record.

The Administrator closes the record, retains it as required by REC-01 (at least 5 years under 17 CCR §54326), and reports any discharge, termination and reasons at the next quality improvement review under GOV-04. If a change affects the plan of operation, the Administrator reports it to CCL within 10 working days, as REC-02 requires.

responsibilities.duty: Applies the entrance and exit criteria, explains move-out terms, coordinates with the service coordinator and authorized representative, completes the transition plan, refund and billing close-out, and record closure.
Report any move request at once, help the individual prepare for the move, take inventory of belongings and funds, and carry out the transition plan.
Leads placement planning, helps identify a new setting, and confirms service authorization changes.
Take part in planning, state their choices, and sign for belongings and funds returned.

documentation: Signed admission agreement including move-out and refund terms
Notes of the move request, planning meeting and options discussed
Written notice of termination (if applicable) with reasons and the efforts to keep the individual
Written transition plan
Health summary and medication transfer record
Belongings and funds inventory signed by the receiving party
Refund statement and billing close-out records
Closing note and notice to the regional center of the departure date

policies.title: Assistance with Self-Administered Medications and Staff Training
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all direct care staff who assist with medications, and licensed professionals who train them
policies.purpose: To make sure medications are stored, assisted with, recorded and disposed of safely and lawfully, and that only properly trained staff assist individuals with their medications.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assists individuals with the self-administration of prescription and nonprescription medications as required by 22 CCR §80075 (C3). Staff assist; they do not administer. Staff do not give injections except as authorized by law; staff designated by the Administrator may assist with self-administration of injections only within what the law allows. Medication is never forced, hidden or camouflaged. As-needed (PRN) medications are handled under the PRN rules in §80075(b)(4)–(6). Staff may assist with metered-dose and dry-powder inhalers only after training by a licensed professional, with written procedures, an annual review by that professional, and a record in the personnel file. Services requiring specialized skills are performed only by licensed or certified personnel, or by an unlicensed person with prior CCL approval where no license or certification exists (22 CCR §85065(f), C6). Staff who assist with medications are at least 18 years old (22 CCR §80065, C4). Staff follow bloodborne pathogen precautions under 29 CFR 1910.1030 when handling sharps or bodily fluids.

definitions.definition: Helping the individual take their own medication, for example by reminding, opening containers, steadying a cup or reading the label, while the individual remains in control.
A medication taken as needed rather than on a fixed schedule, used only as the prescriber's written directions allow.
A locked, facility-controlled place where medications are kept for individuals who need assistance.
A physician, registered nurse or other licensed health professional who is qualified to train and review staff on a medication-related procedure.

procedures: The Administrator assigns medication assistance only to staff who are at least 18 years old, have been oriented to this policy, and have completed the training required for the individual's needs. Staff names are kept on a current list.

Before assisting any individual, staff review the individual's Needs and Services Plan and the physician's written medication orders and check the pharmacy label. Medication is assisted only according to the label and the prescriber's directions.

Staff wash their hands and check the individual's identity, the medication name, dose, time and route against the label and the medication record, then assist the individual to take the medication. The individual's choice and dignity are respected. Staff never force, hide or camouflage medication in food or drink.

If an individual refuses a medication, staff do not force it. Staff record the refusal on the medication record and notify the Administrator. The Administrator notifies the prescriber promptly when advice is needed and documents the call.
Staff record each dose on the medication record immediately after the individual takes it, with date, time and staff initials. Missed doses, refusals and errors are recorded with the reason.

PRN medications are given only when the prescriber's written directions allow it, following §80075(b)(4)–(6). Staff record the reason, time, dose and the result, and contact the prescriber when the directions require.

Staff may assist with metered-dose and dry-powder inhalers only after a licensed professional has trained them. The professional's written procedures, the names of the trained staff and the training date are kept, the professional reviews them annually, and the training is recorded in each trained staff member's personnel file.

Staff do not give injections. Where an individual self-injects, only designated, trained staff may assist as the law allows, and any task needing licensed skill is done by a licensed person arranged through HW-02. Sharps are disposed of in puncture-resistant containers and staff follow the facility's exposure control practices under 29 CFR 1910.1030.

Oxygen use follows §80075(e). The Administrator confirms the physician's order, makes sure signs, safe storage, ventilation and fire precautions are in place, and trains staff on the individual's oxygen equipment before use.

All medications that are centrally stored are kept in a locked space under the temperature and separation conditions on the label, with controlled access, and each individual's medications are kept separate. Storage records are kept at least 1 year.

Medications that are discontinued, expired or not retained by the individual are destroyed only when witnessed by the Administrator and one other adult who is not an individual served. Both sign a record listing the medication, amount and date. The record is kept at least 1 year.

If a medication error occurs, staff first make sure the individual is safe, call the physician, pharmacist or poison control as needed, call 911 for an emergency, and notify the Administrator immediately. The Administrator documents the error, notifies the authorized representative, and reports under BSP-04 and HW-04 if the individual needed medical treatment or if there was a poisoning.
Staff keep a written record of each individual's medication allergies, side effects and the prescriber's contact on the medication record.
The Administrator reviews medication records at least monthly, compares them to the pharmacy supply, and corrects problems. A nurse consultant under HW-02 reviews practices as scheduled.
The Administrator reviews each staff member's competence in medication assistance at hire, after any error, and annually, and documents the review in the personnel file under STF-05.

responsibilities.duty: Assigns and oversees trained staff, makes sure orders, storage, records and destruction follow this policy, and reports errors and incidents.
Assist with self-administration only, record each dose and refusal, store medications securely, and report problems at once.
Train staff on inhalers and other health procedures, review procedures annually, and advise on individual medication questions.
Provide written directions and labels and answer questions about medications.

documentation: Physician's written orders and pharmacy labels
Medication administration/assistance record for each individual
Central storage records (kept at least 1 year)
Record of destruction of medications witnessed by the Administrator and an adult non-client (kept at least 1 year)
Written inhaler procedures, list of trained staff, annual professional review, and training documentation in personnel files
Medication error and refusal records
Monthly Administrator medication review

policies.title: Nursing Oversight, Health Care Coordination and Consultants
policies.applies_to: Administrator, direct care staff, nurse and other consultants
policies.purpose: To make sure each individual gets needed medical and dental care, that services needing specialized skill are delivered only by qualified people, and that nursing, consultant and physician input is coordinated with the regional center and with the individual's plans.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] ensures that each individual receives first aid and needed medical and dental care, including transportation to it (22 CCR §80075, C3). Services requiring specialized skills are performed only by licensed or certified personnel. Where no license or certification exists for a service, [AGENCY NAME] gets prior CCL approval before an unlicensed person provides it (22 CCR §85065(f), C6). The facility provides the consultant hours required by 17 CCR §56004(f) (C22) for its approved service level, which is 8, 12 or 16 hours per consumer per six months as applicable, and lists its consultants in the plan of operation. The Administrator coordinates with the individual's physician, the regional center and any Restricted Health Condition Care Plan under the Needs and Services Plan (22 CCR §85068.2, C8) as described below. The facility supports the individual's right to receive or reject medical care and to take part in decisions about health care.

definitions.definition: A qualified professional, such as a registered nurse, behavior specialist, dietitian or therapist, engaged by the facility to give expert input on individuals' needs.
A plan required in the Needs and Services Plan when an individual has a restricted health condition, built under 22 CCR §80092.2 as referenced in the Needs and Services Plan rule.
A service that needs licensed or certified personnel, for example wound care or a health procedure outside the usual assistance staff give.
Making sure the individual's physician, dentist, specialists, regional center and facility share needed information and follow the same plan.

procedures: Before admission, the Administrator reviews the individual's written medical assessment, functional capabilities assessment and any restricted health condition information, and decides with the service coordinator whether needed health services can be provided. Results are recorded in the Needs and Services Plan.

Within the first 30 days of admission, the Administrator arranges with the individual for a physician and a dentist (keeping the individual's current providers when they wish) and records provider names, phone numbers and appointment schedules in the record.

Staff make sure each individual attends routine, preventive and follow-up medical and dental visits. Staff provide or arrange transportation (see HE-05), accompany the individual where needed, and bring the medication list and recent notes.

After each visit, the staff person records the findings, orders, medication changes and follow-up dates in the record, updates medication records, and reports to the Administrator the same day. The Administrator informs the authorized representative and service coordinator of significant changes.

The Administrator identifies for each individual any service that needs licensed or certified skill. These are arranged through a licensed nurse, home health agency or other licensed provider. Direct care staff do not perform them unless they are licensed or certified for the task.

Where a needed service has no license or certification and an unlicensed person would provide it, the Administrator requests prior written approval from CCL before the person starts, and keeps the approval in the record.

The Administrator engages a registered nurse consultant and other consultants as needed to review health care, advise on individual health needs and train staff. Each consultant has a written agreement stating duties and credentials, and the consultants are listed in the plan of operation.

The Administrator schedules consultant time so that the hours per consumer per six months required by 17 CCR §56004(f) for the facility's approved service level are met, and keeps a log of dates, hours, consumers served and topics for each consultant.

The nurse consultant reviews each individual's health status, medication records, and health risks (including seizures, swallowing problems and choking, see HW-03) at least as often as the consultation agreement states, and gives written recommendations that the Administrator acts on within 10 business days.

If an individual has a restricted health condition, the Administrator builds the Restricted Health Condition Care Plan with the physician and nurse consultant, includes it in the Needs and Services Plan, trains staff on it, and updates it when the condition changes.

The Administrator shares health information with the physician, regional center and others only with consent or as the law allows (see IR-04), and asks the individual or authorized representative to sign a release when needed.

Individuals decide about their own health care as far as they are able. Staff give information in an understandable way, support consent and refusal under IR-05, and record refusals of care. The Administrator notifies the physician of refusals that affect the individual's health.

The Administrator reviews the health care record of each individual at least quarterly with the service coordinator or at each IPP review, checking preventive care, medications, hospital visits, and any unmet needs, and records the results.

If a change of condition occurs, staff follow HW-04 and the Administrator updates the Needs and Services Plan. If a consultant recommends changes in staffing or supports, the Administrator reviews staffing under STF-01.

responsibilities.duty: Arranges medical and dental care and transportation, engages consultants, makes sure specialized services go to licensed or certified persons or CCL-approved persons, and coordinates with the regional center.
Reviews health status and records, advises on health risks, trains staff, and gives written recommendations.
Take individuals to appointments, record outcomes, follow physician orders, and report changes.
Provide medical and dental assessment and treatment and written orders.

documentation: Physician, dentist and specialist contact list and appointment record
Visit summaries, orders and follow-up notes
Consultant agreements and credentials
Consultant log of hours by consumer for each six-month period
Written consultant recommendations and the Administrator's responses
CCL approval letters for unlicensed providers of specialized services (if any)
Restricted Health Condition Care Plan (if applicable)
Quarterly health care review

policies.title: Health Monitoring, Seizures and Choking Risk
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all direct care staff, nurse consultant
policies.purpose: To make sure each individual's health risks, including seizures, swallowing problems and choking, are identified, recorded in the Needs and Services Plan, monitored daily, and handled by trained staff using written individual protocols.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] identifies and records each individual's health risks, including seizures, dysphagia and choking risk, in the Needs and Services Plan (22 CCR §85068.2, C8), which includes the written medical assessment and the functional capabilities assessment. Direct care staff are trained in first aid (22 CCR §80075, C3), and [AGENCY NAME] also requires CPR certification as an agency standard. Specialized care is provided only by licensed or certified personnel or by persons approved by CCL where no license or certification exists (22 CCR §85065(f), C6). Staff are trained on each individual's protocols and the training is documented. Where an individual has a restricted health condition, the facility builds the Restricted Health Condition Care Plan under §80092.2 as the Needs and Services Plan rule requires. Staffing for meals and activities is set to meet these needs (17 CCR §56004, C22).

definitions.definition: A written individual plan, prepared with the physician or nurse consultant, describing the person's seizure types, what staff do, when to call 911 and what to record.
Difficulty swallowing, which may require a modified food texture or liquid consistency or special positioning.
A recorded risk that food, liquid or objects may block the airway, based on assessment, diagnosis, behavior or history.
A condition described in 22 CCR §80092 that requires a Restricted Health Condition Care Plan in the Needs and Services Plan.

procedures: During pre-admission review, the Administrator reads the written medical assessment, the functional capabilities assessment and any physician statements to identify seizures, swallowing difficulty, choking history, allergies, chronic conditions and other health risks, and records them in the Needs and Services Plan.

Within 14 days of admission, the Administrator and nurse consultant write an individual protocol for each identified risk, including signs to watch for, steps staff take, emergency contacts, and when to call 911. The physician reviews the seizure, swallowing and choking protocols.

If swallowing or choking risk is suspected but not yet assessed, the Administrator arranges for a physician or swallowing specialist evaluation. Until a diet order is received, staff give food in the form already ordered, supervise the individual at meals, and tell the cook.

Staff receive training on each individual's protocols before working alone with that individual, and again whenever a protocol changes. The trainer, date, staff names and content are recorded in the training file and personnel file.

Direct care staff complete first-aid training as required by 22 CCR §80075 and CPR certification as an agency requirement, before working alone with individuals. Certificates are kept in personnel files, and the Administrator tracks expiration dates.

Staff observe each individual daily for changes in alertness, eating, swallowing, breathing, skin, mobility, mood and seizure activity, and record observations in consumer notes. Anything unusual is reported to the Administrator the same shift.

During a seizure, staff stay with the individual, note the time it began, protect the individual from injury, loosen tight clothing, place the individual on their side when the seizure ends, and put nothing in the mouth. Staff call 911 when the individual's protocol says so or when the seizure is unusually long, repeats, the individual is injured, has trouble breathing or does not wake, or it is the individual's first seizure.

After a seizure, staff record the date, time, duration, description, triggers, injuries, care given and recovery on the seizure record, and tell the Administrator. The Administrator informs the physician as the protocol requires and the authorized representative.

For meals, staff follow the diet order and the individual's feeding protocol, including food texture, liquid consistency, pace, position, supervision level and assistive equipment. Staff stay with individuals who have a choking risk throughout the meal. See HE-04.

If an individual chokes, staff use the first-aid and CPR techniques they were trained in, call 911 if the airway is not cleared at once or if the individual loses consciousness, and stay with the individual. Staff record what happened and tell the Administrator immediately.

The Administrator reports an injury or event needing medical treatment under HW-04 (CCL by the next working day, written report within 7 days) and in BSP-04. The individual's physician is notified and the protocol is reviewed after every serious event.

Services needing licensed or certified skill (for example suctioning, tube feeding or other health procedures) are done only by licensed or certified persons arranged through HW-02, or by a person CCL has approved in advance if no license or certification exists. Staff who are not qualified do not perform them.

If the individual has a restricted health condition, the Administrator builds the Restricted Health Condition Care Plan with the physician, includes it in the Needs and Services Plan, trains staff on it, and reviews it at each change of condition.

The Administrator checks staffing for meals, bathing, community outings and overnight so that supervision matches individual risks. If risks require added staff, the Administrator requests it from the service coordinator and adjusts the staffing plan under STF-01.

The nurse consultant reviews the seizure, swallowing and choking protocols at least every six months and whenever a seizure, choking event or hospital visit occurs. The Administrator updates the Needs and Services Plan and retrains staff within 10 business days.

responsibilities.duty: Identifies risks, writes and updates protocols, makes sure training is done and documented, reports events, and adjusts staffing.
Helps develop and review protocols, trains staff, and advises on health monitoring.
Know and follow each individual's protocols, supervise meals, respond to seizures and choking, observe and record, and report.
Assess, diagnose, order diets and treatment, and approve protocols.

documentation: Health risks recorded in the Needs and Services Plan
Individual seizure, swallowing and choking protocols with physician and nurse review
Restricted Health Condition Care Plan (if applicable)
Staff training records for individual protocols, first aid and CPR certificates
Seizure records and choking incident records
Consumer notes of daily health observations
Incident reports and reports to CCL
Six-month protocol reviews

policies.title: Change of Condition and Emergency Medical Care
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all direct care staff including night staff
policies.purpose: To make sure staff recognize a change in an individual's condition, get emergency or urgent medical care without delay, notify the right people, report to CCL on time, and update the individual's plan afterward.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps first-aid supplies and an emergency contact list, and has an emergency communication person available at all times (22 CCR §80075(g)–(h), C3). Night staff are able to help in an emergency and are trained in the facility's planned emergency procedures and first aid (22 CCR §85065.6, C7). The facility reports to CCL by the next working day, with a written report within 7 days, any injury needing medical treatment, poisoning, epidemic outbreak or other event listed in 22 CCR §80061 (C1). The authorized representative and service coordinator are told of significant changes. The Needs and Services Plan is updated after any change of condition (22 CCR §85068.2, C8).

definitions.definition: A noticeable change in an individual's physical, mental, emotional or behavioral status, such as a new illness, injury, loss of function, new pain, refusal to eat, sudden confusion or behavior change.
A situation that threatens life or health and needs immediate medical care, such as unresponsiveness, trouble breathing, chest pain, stroke signs, severe bleeding, a prolonged seizure or poisoning.
The person available at all times who can be reached for emergency communication and has the contact list.
The next day on which CCL offices are open, counted from the day the event occurred or was discovered.

procedures: The Administrator keeps first-aid supplies in an easily reached place, checks them monthly against the list required by 22 CCR §80075(g), replaces used or expired items, and records the check.

An emergency contact list is posted near the phone and kept in each shift's binder. It includes 911, poison control, each individual's physician, the pharmacy, the authorized representatives, the service coordinator, the Administrator, the emergency communication person, the CCL office and the nurse consultant. The Administrator updates it at least every quarter.

The Administrator names an emergency communication person for every day and every hour, including nights and weekends, and publishes the schedule to staff. Staff on every shift know how to reach that person.

Night staff (10 p.m. to 7 a.m.) complete training in the facility's emergency procedures and first aid before working a night shift alone. Where a signal system is required, a named staff person is responsible for responding to it.

When staff observe a change of condition, they check on the individual, give first aid within their training, and call the Administrator or on-call person. If the situation is an emergency, staff call 911 first and then notify the Administrator.

If the situation is not an emergency but needs medical advice, staff call the individual's physician, the nurse consultant or urgent care, and follow the instructions. Staff record the advice and who gave it.

A staff member stays with the individual until the situation is resolved. Staff send or bring the medication list, health summary, physician and representative contacts and insurance information with the individual to the hospital or clinic. Staff arrange transportation (ambulance or facility transport) as needed.

Staff notify the authorized representative and the service coordinator as soon as possible, and in any event the same day for any emergency, hospital visit or significant change. The staff person records the date, time, person reached and what was said.

The Administrator decides whether the event must be reported. Within the next working day, the Administrator reports to CCL by phone, email or the reporting method CCL requires, any injury needing medical treatment, any poisoning, any epidemic outbreak, any death, any use of an automated external defibrillator, and any unusual incident or absence that threatens an individual's health or safety, as listed in §80061.

Epidemic outbreaks are also reported immediately to the local fire authority, and to the local health officer when appropriate, as §80061 requires. Poisonings and other events listed in §80061 are also reported to the local health officer when appropriate.

Within 7 days of the event, the Administrator sends CCL a written report that gives the individual's name, age, sex and admission date, the date and nature of the event, the physician's findings and treatment, and the disposition. A copy of the reports that §80061 requires is given to the authorized representative.

The Administrator also reports to the regional center as BSP-04 and REC-02 require. If the event may involve abuse or neglect, staff follow BSP-03, including the 2-hour and 24-hour reports to the ombudsman, CCL and law enforcement as required. If an individual dies, staff follow HW-05.

Within 3 business days after a change of condition or a return from a hospital, the Administrator reviews discharge instructions with the physician or nurse consultant, updates medication records and protocols, and trains staff on any new care.

The Administrator updates the Needs and Services Plan after each significant change of condition, with input from the individual, the authorized representative, the physician and the service coordinator. If the individual's needs now exceed what the facility can meet, the Administrator follows PCS-04.

The Administrator reviews each emergency event within 10 business days to see whether staffing, training, equipment or supplies need to change, and records corrective steps for the quality improvement review in GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains first-aid supplies, contact list and emergency communication coverage, decides on and files reports to CCL and the regional center, updates the Needs and Services Plan, and reviews events.
Recognize changes in condition, give first aid, call 911 or the physician as needed, notify the Administrator and record events.
Stay reachable at all hours and help staff reach emergency services and contacts.
Advise on changes of condition and on follow-up care.

documentation: First-aid supply checklist (monthly)
Posted and binder emergency contact list and emergency communication person schedule
Night staff emergency procedure and first-aid training records
Change-of-condition and emergency notes in consumer notes
Notification log for the authorized representative and service coordinator
CCL next-working-day report record and 7-day written report
Regional center special incident report where required
Updated Needs and Services Plan and post-event review

policies.title: Death of an Individual
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all direct care staff, on-call manager, and any staff who are with a resident at the facility, in the community, or at a hospital or day program
policies.purpose: To make sure that when a resident dies, [AGENCY NAME] responds with dignity and care, notifies the right people on time, preserves the records and protects other residents. The policy also sets out how the facility meets its reporting duties to Community Care Licensing (CCL), the regional center and the authorized representative, and how the facility reviews each death to learn from it.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports every death of a resident to CCL by the next working day and sends a written report within 7 days (22 CCR §80061). This applies whether the death occurs in the facility, in a hospital, on an outing, at a day program or anywhere else. Deaths from injury, abuse or other than natural causes are reported the same way, and any suspected abuse is also reported under WIC §15630 within the 2-hour or 24-hour time limits. The facility notifies the resident's authorized representative and the vendoring regional center, and reports the death to the regional center as a Special Incident Report (SIR) under 17 CCR §54327. The Administrator will confirm the current text of §54327 with the regional center, including any changes effective May 1, 2026, and follows whichever notice requirement is stricter. After a death, the facility preserves all records, protects the person's property and completes a mortality review.

definitions.definition: The person legally authorized to act for the resident, such as a conservator, parent of a minor, or a person the resident has designated, as recorded in the resident's file.
A death resulting from injury, abuse, neglect, accident, suicide, overdose, poisoning or any circumstance that is not clearly the result of illness or the natural end of life.
The next day on which CCL's offices are open for business, not counting weekends and state holidays.
A Special Incident Report submitted to the vendoring regional center under 17 CCR §54327.
A written internal review of the circumstances of a death, the care provided, and any lessons or corrective actions.

procedures: Staff who find a resident unresponsive or not breathing call 911 immediately and begin CPR and use the AED unless a valid advance directive, DNR or POLST form is in the resident's file. Staff give that form to emergency responders. Staff trained under HW-04 follow dispatcher instructions until responders arrive.

The staff member on duty notifies the Administrator or on-call manager by phone right away. Staff do not wait until the end of the shift. The staff member stays with the resident and other residents until relief arrives.

Staff follow the instructions of paramedics, law enforcement and the coroner or medical examiner. If the death was unexpected, or abuse, neglect or an accident is suspected, staff do not move or clean anything in the area unless responders direct them to. Staff note who was present and what they saw.

If a resident dies away from the facility (hospital, outing, day program or transport), the staff member with the resident, or the first staff member told of the death, calls the Administrator right away. The same notification and reporting steps below apply.

The Administrator (or on-call manager) personally notifies the authorized representative by phone as soon as possible. The Administrator does not use text or email for first notice. If the representative cannot be reached, the Administrator keeps trying and documents each attempt and the time.

The Administrator notifies the regional center service coordinator, or the regional center's after-hours line, by phone immediately. The Administrator then submits the SIR in the format and within the time limits required by 17 CCR §54327. [AGENCY NAME] uses the 24-hour initial notice and 48-hour written report timelines in place before May 1, 2026 unless the regional center confirms a different timeline under the amended rule.

The Administrator reports the death to CCL by phone or email to the licensing office by the next working day, as required by 22 CCR §80061. The Administrator sends the written report on the CCL incident form (LIC 624 or the current form) within 7 days.

The written report states: the resident's name, age, sex and admission date; the date and nature of the event; physician findings and treatment (including the hospital's or coroner's findings when available); and the disposition. The Administrator provides a copy to the authorized representative and to the regional center, in line with §80061(f)-(i).

If the death may have resulted from physical abuse, the Administrator ensures a report is made to the local ombudsman, CCL and law enforcement within 2 hours if serious bodily injury is suspected, and within 24 hours otherwise, under WIC §15630 and §80061(c)-(d). The Administrator follows BSP-03 and removes any suspected staff member from duty with residents pending investigation.

If the death is reported as an epidemic outbreak, poisoning or catastrophe, or is related to one, the Administrator also makes the additional reports required by §80061, including to the local health officer when appropriate and to the local fire authority immediately for an epidemic outbreak.
